newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo announces plans to reform banks.
newsitem.headline: Yugo announces plans to reform banks.

text.p: The Yugoslav government announced on Wednesday plans to restructure and privatise the country's insolvent banking system in 1997.
Banks have not undergone reform in previous years and now they will be restructured, Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Jovan Zebic told journalists.
Zebic added the government would also seek help from the World Bank for the banking sector reform.

Outlining its plan in four short paragraphs of the 24-page economic policy paper, the government also said it planned to attract foreign banks to establish their presence in Yugoslavia, directly or through their affiliates.

"The government aims to rehabilitate and privatise banks, along with downsizing the entire sector, to make it more efficient and competitive with foreign banks," said the official 1997 economic policy paper presented to journalists.
To resolve the problem of the so-called old hard currency savings, the government said it planned to convert hard currency deposits into banks' shares.

The paper gave no figures, but according to the last report issued in June by the Association of Yugoslav Banks, the state owed its citizens 6.6 billion German marks in hard currency savings frozen in the early 1990's.
Yugoslav Finance Minister Tomica Raicevic said the government will prepare a law on hard currency savings and present it to the parliament within next four months.
But analysts doubted the government will come up with a solution so soon.

"They only say so. They may even send the bill to the parliament, but they'll find excuses to send it back to the government to amend it and delay its adoption," an analyst who asked not to be named told Reuters. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
